clinicalPearls: A common, benign bony outgrowth (exostosis) arising in the midline of the hard palate
Presents as a slow-growing, bony-hard, sessile or lobulated swelling covered by normal mucosa
More frequent in females and shows variation in prevalence between ethnic groups
Usually asymptomatic and often discovered incidentally
The thin overlying mucosa is prone to traumatic ulceration that can be slow to heal
Its main clinical importance lies in interference with the fitting and construction of dentures
The diagnosis is clinical; a hard midline palatal swelling with normal mucosa needs no biopsy
No treatment is required unless prosthetic needs, recurrent trauma, or patient concern warrant surgical removal
reference.pathophysiology: A torus palatinus is a developmental, benign exostosis composed of dense cortical bone with a variable amount of trabecular bone, arising along the midline palatal suture. Its growth is slow and it typically becomes apparent from adolescence or early adulthood; both genetic predisposition and functional or masticatory factors have been proposed as contributors. The lesion is not neoplastic and has no malignant potential, and the thin mucosa stretched over the bony prominence is easily traumatised, which accounts for the occasional ulceration seen clinically.
additionalDifferentials: Torus mandibularis and other oral exostoses
Salivary gland tumour of the palate such as pleomorphic adenoma
Squamous cell carcinoma or other palatal neoplasm if the mucosa is abnormal
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination confirming a bony-hard midline swelling with normal overlying mucosa
Palpation to assess consistency, extent, and mucosal integrity
Radiographs or cross-sectional imaging only if the diagnosis is uncertain or for surgical planning
Study models for denture planning when a prosthesis is required
Biopsy reserved for lesions with atypical, non-bony, ulcerated, or soft features
Review of the mucosa for traumatic ulceration
redFlags: Ulceration that fails to heal or shows induration, raising suspicion of neoplasia
Rapid growth, which is atypical for a torus
A soft or fluctuant rather than bony-hard swelling suggesting another lesion
Signs of infection or abscess formation
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent as the torus is entirely benign; although it continues to grow slowly it causes no harm, and surgical removal, when indicated, is generally curative with uncommon recurrence.
pitfalls: Mistaking a torus for a neoplasm or abscess and over-investigating
Missing a genuine palatal tumour by assuming any midline swelling is a torus
Traumatising the thin overlying mucosa during denture fitting
Recommending surgery when observation would suffice
references: Cawson's Essentials of Oral Pathology and Oral Medicine
management: Reassure that the lesion is a benign bony exostosis with no malignant potential and needs no treatment when asymptomatic
Observation with periodic review, as intervention is unnecessary for the incidental, asymptomatic torus
Manage traumatic ulceration of the thin overlying mucosa with local protective measures until healing
Surgical reduction or excision reserved for tori that interfere with denture construction, cause recurrent ulceration, or impair speech and function
Take study models and involve prosthodontics when a denture is required over a prominent torus
Biopsy only if features become atypical, non-bony, or fail to heal, to exclude other pathology
